answer.label: Not Confucius — an old Chinese proverb
answer.authorDates: In English print by 1853 · the saying is credited to Ming scholar Jiao Hong (1540–1620)
answer.sourceLine: There is no basis for the Confucius attribution: the line appears nowhere in the Analects. It is an old Chinese proverb — Archbishop Richard Chenevix Trench printed it in English as “Better a diamond with a flaw, than a pebble without one” in his 1853 Proverbs and Their Lessons, expressly calling it a “Chinese proverb,” not a saying of Confucius. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed and traces the underlying saying to Ming-dynasty scholar Jiao Hong (1540–1620).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Richard Chenevix Trench, 1853 — who calls it “this Chinese proverb”
An anonymous Chinese proverb; traced by Wikiquote to Ming scholar Jiao Hong (1540–1620)
The Analects, or any genuine work of Confucius

source.excerpt: And in this Chinese proverb which follows, ‘Better a diamond with a flaw, than a pebble without one,’ there is, to my mind, the assertion of a great Christian truth, and of one which reaches deep down to the very foundations of Christian morality — the more valuable as coming to us from a people beyond the range and reach of the influences of direct Revelation.
trail: In Proverbs and Their Lessons (1853), Archbishop Richard Chenevix Trench quotes “Better a diamond with a flaw, than a pebble without one” and calls it plainly “this Chinese proverb” — no mention of Confucius.

Wikiquote files the line under Misattributed, noting it was pinned on Confucius in a 1967 general-knowledge book and is “in fact… a Chinese saying by a Confucian scholar of the Ming Dynasty, Jiao Hong (1540–1620).”
A Boston University Core Curriculum note likewise flags it as “often attributed to Confucius,” while observing it does not appear in the Analects and likely derives from a Chinese proverb.
The line is absent from the Analects and from every authenticated work of Confucius; the earliest hard evidence is Trench’s 1853 book, and the modern “Confucius” tag is a 20th-century graft.

source.excerptNote: Trench’s 1853 wording keeps the final “one”; the modern viral form drops it to “… a pebble without.” Note that Trench presents it as a Chinese proverb — not a saying of Confucius.

source.rightsNote: The English wording is documented in Richard Chenevix Trench’s Proverbs and Their Lessons, first published in 1853 — long before the 1931 U.S. copyright cutoff — and the underlying Chinese proverb is far older, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Jiao Hong (焦竑)
author.heading: Not Confucius — a Ming-era Chinese saying
author.bio: Jiao Hong was a scholar-official of the late Ming dynasty who placed first (zhuangyuan) in the 1589 imperial examination and served in the Hanlin Academy. A philosopher and historian, he compiled the biographical collection Guochao xianzheng lu, regarded as an important supplement to the official History of Ming. Wikiquote credits the “diamond with a flaw” saying to him; in English the proverb has long circulated anonymously, as Trench recorded it in 1853.

misattribution.heading: A proverb wearing a philosopher’s name
misattribution.intro: Feel-good lines gravitate to Confucius, and this one is a textbook case: a genuine Chinese proverb re-labelled as his personal wisdom.

items.why: The line is in none of the Analects or other authentic Confucian texts. Wikiquote places it in its Misattributed section and notes an early appearance in a 1967 general-knowledge compendium — not in Confucius.
Archbishop Richard Chenevix Trench recorded it in English as a “Chinese proverb” in Proverbs and Their Lessons (1853), with no attribution to Confucius.
Wikiquote traces the saying to this late-Ming philosopher and historian — a figure who lived roughly two thousand years after Confucius.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: an old Chinese proverb, printed in English by Trench in 1853 and traced by Wikiquote to Ming scholar Jiao Hong — not a saying of Confucius.

context.heading: Why the label sticks
lead: The sentiment — that flawed substance beats flawless emptiness — reads as timeless moral wisdom, which is exactly the register the internet associates with Confucius. That cultural shorthand, plus the saying’s genuine Chinese origin, made the misattribution almost frictionless.

Trench’s 1853 discussion is telling: he cited the proverb precisely because it came “from a people beyond the range… of direct Revelation” — i.e. as anonymous folk wisdom, not the pronouncement of a named sage.
detailsBody: The modern viral wording drops Trench’s final “one” (“… a pebble without”), a small smoothing typical of quotes that have travelled through decades of reposting.
context.pull: A real Chinese proverb, re-badged with the internet’s favorite Chinese name.
